anf_compare.notes: Translated from the PG 74 Greek; no published English version was used for wording.

bible_refs.note: Paraphrased in indirect speech: τῷ μὲν νοῒ δουλεύειν τῷ θείῳ… νόμῳ, τῇ δὲ σαρκὶ νόμῳ ἁμαρτίας.
Τὸ γὰρ θέλειν παράκειταί μοι, τὸ δὲ κατεργάζεσθαι τὸ καλὸν οὔ.
Lemma (first half) and the later 'has set me free' (ἠλευθέρωσέ με); 'law of sin and death' is from the same verse.
Quoted closely; Cyril's text lacks ἑαυτοῦ after εἰς τὴν σάρκα ('his own flesh'), so the English follows his wording.
Clear allusion: sealed with the Holy Spirit (ἐσφραγίσθητε τῷ πνεύματι… τῷ ἁγίῳ).
Lemma, first half only; Cyril comments on its incomplete syntax in u06-rem-early.

choices.why: κεκλήμεθα… εἰς ἐλεύθερον ἀξίωμα may echo Galatians 5:13 (ἐπ' ἐλευθερίᾳ ἐκλήθητε); possible allusion only, so not cited inline. Cyril marks it 'as I said', pointing back to his own earlier wording.
τοῖς τοῦ θανάτου… βρόχοις ('snares of death') is close to the Psalms' language (e.g. Psalm 18:5, LXX 17:6, which reads ὠδῖνες/παγίδες), but the wording does not match; not cited.

choices.term: τό γε ἧκον εἰς νοῦν καὶ τὴν ἐν αὐτῷ θέλησιν
choices.why: τό γε ἧκον εἰς νοῦν καὶ τὴν ἐν αὐτῷ θέλησιν is adverbial ('so far as the mind and its will were concerned'), with τὸ ἑλέσθαι … δουλεύειν as the subject of ἐνυπῆρχεν; πάλαι here means before Christ, so 'formerly' / 'even before' rather than 'long ago'.

choices.english: the flesh forced us toward sin
choices.why: κατεβιάζετο … ἡ σάρξ is middle with active sense, as in u05-rem-mid (καταβιάζεται … τὸν νοῦν); the unexpressed object is us (ἡμῖν above), so 'the flesh forced us toward sin'.
τὸ σαρκικὸν φρόνημα rendered 'the fleshly way of thinking' so it is not confused with νοῦς ('mind'), which this passage sets against the flesh.

pass_a_gloss: [continuing] mind (dianoia) of man, the evil leading-out-against (antexagontos) it; and he maintained (diischurizeto) that the mind of the more-equitable (epieikesteroi) is-vexed (aschallei) sometimes being tyrannised (tyrannoumenos) by the passions (pathe) of the flesh, and is greatly distraught (alyei) and being-weak is-ashamed; yet to unburden (apophortisasthai) the unwilled (abouleton) sin it has from nowhere, pleasure falling-upon terribly. Therefore also it is-weak toward resistance (antistasis), helped toward this not at all through the law. Truly then the divine (thespesios) Paul speaks if he maintains to serve with mind the divine law, with flesh law of sin; and this I think is what he said 'For to will (thelein) lies-near me, but to work-out (katergazesthai) the good not.' Of old then, as I said, there was-in us what pertains to mind and the will in it, to choose (helesthai) to serve the divine law, but the flesh forced (katebiazeto) toward sin as-it-were raising-up-against its own will (thelema). There was then condemnation (katakrima) for those wishing to complete the good, but not able because of being tyrannised by passions; but in Christ the condemning has ceased (pepautai), that is the overreaching (pleonexia) of the fleshly movements (kinemata). [Rom 8:2] For the law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus. Necessary I think for exact clarification of the thoughts in these to say that: as he names the fleshly mind-set (phronema) law of sin and death, carrying us toward every form of baseness (phaulotes), so also law of spirit of life the spiritual will, that is the inclination (rhope) of the mind toward the good; but [Gal 6:8] the one sowing into the flesh from the flesh will reap corruption (phthora), the one sowing into the spirit from the spirit will reap life eternal. So the law of the spirit of life, that is the will of the mind carrying to life, was in us also of old; for we served with mind law of God; but it was-sick, as I said, the feebleness (to adranes) toward resistance, and being defeated by the desires (epithymiai) of flesh was condemned by the law. But since having cast off the being-sick it was strengthened (errhosthe) through Christ; for we have been sealed (katesphragismetha) through him with the Holy Spirit, and have put on (emphiesmetha) the 'power from on high', therefore also we have been redeemed, and are yoked no longer to evil; we have been called, as I said, to free rank (axioma). So the law of the spirit of life, that is the will of the mind, inclined to good-working (agathourgia) and carrying to life, when it has been enriched with the grace through Christ, and freed from the ancient weakness (astheneia), then disregarding the evils from sin and prevailing-over (kateumegethesas) the law of the flesh, freed me, he says; and not itself at all giving the freedom, but rather having become for us procurer (proxenos) of the freedom through Christ. As those under the law of sin by all necessity are bound in the nooses (brochoi) of death, so those who have come outside it, freed through Christ, must again be outside death, and seen better than corruption, and live in sanctification (hagiasmos). [Rom 8:3] For the impossible/inability (to adynaton) of the law in which it was weak through the flesh. Admirable (axiagastos) indeed the [continues: mystagogue].
pass_b_english: …human mind to endure, while evil is ranged against it. He insisted that the mind of the more upright is at times distressed when it is tyrannized by the passions of the flesh, that it is deeply troubled and ashamed of its weakness; yet it has no means at all of throwing off the burden of the sin it does not want, since pleasure falls upon it so fiercely. That is why it is too weak to resist, receiving no help whatever toward this, at least from the law.

So the inspired Paul speaks the truth when he insists that with the mind he serves the divine law, but with the flesh the law of sin (Romans 7:25); and this, I think, is what he meant when he said, “For willing lies close at hand for me, but accomplishing the good does not” (Romans 7:18). Formerly, then, as I said, so far as the mind and the will within it were concerned, we had the choice to serve the divine law; but the flesh forced us toward sin, raising up its own will in opposition, as it were. So there was, then, condemnation for those who wished to accomplish the good but were not able, because they were tyrannized by the passions; but in Christ what condemned has come to an end, that is, the domination of the fleshly impulses.

“For the law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:2). To make the ideas in these words perfectly clear, I think it necessary to say this: just as he calls the fleshly way of thinking, which carries us off toward every kind of wickedness, the law of sin and death, so he calls the spiritual will, that is, the mind’s inclination toward the good, the law of the spirit of life. But “the one who sows to the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, while the one who sows to the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit” (Galatians 6:8).

So the law of the spirit of life, that is, the will of the mind that carries us toward life, was in us even before, for with the mind we served the law of God; but, as I said, it was sick, powerless to resist, and, overcome by the desires of the flesh, it was condemned by the law. But since it has cast off its sickness and been made strong through Christ — for through him we have been sealed with the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13) and have been clothed with “power from on high” (Luke 24:49) — for this reason we have been redeemed and are no longer yoked to evil, but, as I said, we have been called to the dignity of freedom.

So the law of the spirit of life, that is, the will of the mind, which inclines toward doing good and carries us toward life, once it has been enriched with the grace that comes through Christ and set free from its ancient weakness, then, disregarding the evils that come from sin and prevailing over the law of the flesh, “has set me free,” he says (Romans 8:2). Not that it gives the freedom by itself, of course; rather, it has become for us the one who procures the freedom that comes through Christ. And just as those under the law of sin must, by every necessity, also be bound in the snares of death, so those who have come out from sin and been set free through Christ must in turn be beyond death, be seen to be above corruption, and live in holiness.

ἀνθρώπου διάνοιαν, ἀντεξάγοντος αὐτῇ τοῦ κακοῦ· διισχυρίζετο δὲ ὡς ἀσχάλλει μὲν
ἔσθ' ὅτε τῶν ἐπιεικεστέρων ὁ νοῦς τοῖς τῆς σαρκὸς πάθεσι τυραννούμενος, ἀλύει δὲ
σφόδρα καὶ ἀσθενῶν αἰσχύνεται· τὸ γεμὴν ἀποφορτίσασθαι τὴν ἀβούλητον ἁμαρτίαν
οὐδαμόθεν ἔχει, δεινῶς κατεμπιπτούσης τῆς ἡδονῆς. ταύτῃτοι καὶ ἀσθενεῖ πρὸς
ἀντίστασιν, οὐδὲν τὸ παράπαν διά γε τοῦ νόμου πρὸς τοῦτο ἐπικουρούμενος. ἀληθεύει
δὴ οὖν ὁ θεσπέσιος Παῦλος εἰ τῷ μὲν νοῒ δουλεύειν τῷ θείῳ διισχυρίσαιτο νόμῳ, τῇ δὲ
σαρκὶ νόμῳ ἁμαρτίας· καὶ τοῦτο οἶμαί ἐστιν ὅπερ ἔφη "Τὸ γὰρ "θέλειν παράκειταί μοι,
τὸ δὲ κατεργάζεσθαι τὸ καλὸν οὔ." 210 πάλαι μὲν οὖν, ὡς ἔφην, ἐνυπῆρχεν ἡμῖν τό γε
ἧκον εἰς νοῦν καὶ τὴν ἐν αὐτῷ θέλησιν, τὸ ἑλέσθαι τῷ θείῳ δουλεύειν νόμῳ,
κατεβιάζετο δὲ πρὸς ἁμαρτίαν ἡ σὰρξ τὸ οἰκεῖον ὥσπερ ἀντανιστᾶσα θέλημα. ἦν οὖν
ἄρα κατάκριμα τοῖς ἐθέλουσι μὲν ἀποπεραίνειν τὸ ἀγαθὸν, οὐ μὴν ἔτι καὶ δυναμένοις
διὰ τὸ τυραννεῖσθαι τοῖς πάθεσιν· ἀλλ' ἐν Χριστῷ πέπαυται τὸ κατακρίνον, τουτέστιν ἡ
τῶν σαρκικῶν κινημάτων πλεονεξία. Ὁ γὰρ νόμος τοῦ πνεύματος τῆς ζωῆς ἐν Χριστῷ
Ἰησοῦ.
Ἀναγκαῖον δὲ οἶμαι πρὸς ἀκριβῆ διασάφησιν τῶν ἐν τούτοις ἐννοιῶν ἐκεῖνο
εἰπεῖν· ὥσπερ γὰρ ἁμαρτίας καὶ θανάτου νόμον τὸ σαρκικὸν ὀνομάζει φρόνημα, πρὸς
πᾶν εἶδος φαυλότητος ἀποφέρον ἡμᾶς, οὕτω καὶ νόμον πνεύματος ζωῆς τὸ θέλημα τὸ
πνευματικὸν, τουτέστι τὴν εἴς γε τὸ ἀγαθὸν τῆς διανοίας ῥοπήν· ἀλλ' "ὁ μὲν σπείρων εἰς
τὴν σάρκα ἐκ τῆς "σαρκὸς θερίσει φθοράν· ὁ δὲ σπείρων εἰς τὸ πνεῦμα ἐκ "τοῦ
πνεύματος θερίσει ζωὴν αἰώνιον." οὐκοῦν ὁ μὲν νόμος τοῦ πνεύματος τῆς ζωῆς,
τουτέστι τὸ θέλημα τοῦ νοῦ τὸ ἀποφέρον εἰς ζωὴν, ἦν μὲν ἐν ἡμῖν καὶ πάλαι·
ἐδουλεύομεν γὰρ τῷ νοῒ νόμῳ Θεοῦ· ἀλλ' ἠῤῥώστησεν, ὡς ἔφην, τὸ ἀδρανὲς εἰς
ἀντίστασιν, καὶ ταῖς τῆς σαρκὸς ἐπιθυμίαις ἡττώμενος κατεκρίνετο τῷ νόμῳ. ἐπειδὴ δὲ
τὸ νοσεῖν ἀποβαλὼν, ἐῤῥώσθη διὰ Χριστοῦ· κατεσφραγίσμεθα γὰρ δι' αὐτοῦ τῷ Ἁγίῳ
Πνεύματι, καὶ τὴν "ἐξ ὕψους δύναμιν" ἠμφιέσμεθα, ταύτῃτοι καὶ λελυτρώμεθα, καὶ
ὑπεζεύγμεθα μὲν οὐκ ἔτι τῷ κακῷ· κεκλήμεθα δὲ, ὡς ἔφην, εἰς ἐλεύθερον ἀξίωμα.
οὐκοῦν ὁ νόμος τοῦ πνεύματος τῆς ζωῆς, τουτέστι τὸ θέλημα τοῦ νοῦ, τὸ νενευκὸς εἰς
ἀγαθουργίαν καὶ εἰς ζωὴν ἀποφέρον, ὅτε τὴν διὰ Χριστοῦ πεπλούτηκε χάριν, καὶ τῆς
ἀρχαίας ἀσθενείας 211 ἀπήλλακται, τότε τῶν ἐξ ἁμαρτίας ἀλογήσας κακῶν καὶ τοῦ τῆς
σαρκὸς κατευμεγεθήσας νόμου, ἠλευθέρωσέ με, φησί· καὶ οὐκ αὐτός που πάντως τὴν
ἐλευθερίαν διδοὺς, γεγονὼς δὲ μᾶλλον ἡμῖν ἐλευθερίας πρόξενος τῆς διὰ Χριστοῦ.
ὥσπερ δὲ τοὺς ὑπὸ νόμον ὄντας τὸν τῆς ἁμαρτίας πᾶσά πως ἀνάγκη καὶ τοῖς τοῦ
θανάτου καταδεσμεῖσθαι βρόχοις, οὕτω τοὺς ἔξω γεγονότας αὐτῆς, ἠλευθερωμένους τε
διὰ Χριστοῦ, δεῖ δὴ πάλιν ἔξω τε εἶναι θανάτου, καὶ ἀμείνους ὁρᾶσθαι φθορᾶς, καὶ ζῆν
ἐν ἁγιασμῷ. Τὸ γὰρ ἀδύνατον τοῦ νόμου ἐν ᾧ ἠσθένει διὰ τῆς σαρκός. Ἀξιάγαστος μὲν ὁ
reviewer: claude (Wave A review, clause by clause against the Greek)
review_notes: Wrong referent: in τοὺς ἔξω γεγονότας αὐτῆς the feminine αὐτῆς is sin, not the (masculine) law, so 'come out from under it' became 'come out from sin'. Syntax: τό γε ἧκον εἰς νοῦν καὶ τὴν ἐν αὐτῷ θέλησιν is adverbial ('so far as the mind and its will were concerned') with τὸ ἑλέσθαι as subject, and πάλαι means before Christ ('Formerly', 'even before'), not 'long ago'. κατεβιάζετο … ἡ σάρξ is middle with active sense as in u05-rem-mid, so 'the flesh forced us toward sin' instead of 'forced its way'. τὸ σαρκικὸν φρόνημα rendered 'the fleshly way of thinking' so it is not confused with νοῦς ('mind'). 'tyrannised' brought to American spelling. Romans 7:18, 7:25, 8:2, 8:3, Galatians 6:8, Ephesians 1:13 and Luke 24:49 verified; Galatians 6:8 bible_refs note corrected (Cyril's text lacks ἑαυτοῦ).
Copy-text: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos via Khazarzar (Fragmenta in sancti Pauli epistulam ad Romanos.pdf).
Section opens mid-sentence, continuing the last sentence of u05-rem-close (… τὴν | ἀνθρώπου διάνοιαν); rendered with a leading ellipsis.

τὸ ἀδύνατον τοῦ νόμου (Romans 8:3): rendered 'the law's inability' rather than 'what the law could not do', because Cyril goes on to gloss it as τὸ ἀσθενοῦν, 'the weakness', and argues that the sentence lacks a main verb.
κεκλήμεθα… εἰς ἐλεύθερον ἀξίωμα may echo Galatians 5:13 (ἐπ' ἐλευθερίᾳ ἐκλήθητε); possible allusion only, so not cited inline. Cyril marks it 'as I said', pointing back to his own earlier wording.
τοῖς τοῦ θανάτου… βρόχοις ('snares of death') is close to the Psalms' language (e.g. Psalm 18:5, LXX 17:6, which reads ὠδῖνες/παγίδες), but the wording does not match; not cited.
Page numbers 210 and 211 are edition apparatus and are omitted.
Section ends mid-sentence (Ἀξιάγαστος μὲν ὁ | μυσταγωγός…); the sentence continues at the start of u06-rem-early.

τό γε ἧκον εἰς νοῦν καὶ τὴν ἐν αὐτῷ θέλησιν is adverbial ('so far as the mind and its will were concerned'), with τὸ ἑλέσθαι … δουλεύειν as the subject of ἐνυπῆρχεν; πάλαι here means before Christ, so 'formerly' / 'even before' rather than 'long ago'.
κατεβιάζετο … ἡ σάρξ is middle with active sense, as in u05-rem-mid (καταβιάζεται … τὸν νοῦν); the unexpressed object is us (ἡμῖν above), so 'the flesh forced us toward sin'.
τὸ σαρκικὸν φρόνημα rendered 'the fleshly way of thinking' so it is not confused with νοῦς ('mind'), which this passage sets against the flesh.
in τοὺς ἔξω γεγονότας αὐτῆς the feminine αὐτῆς refers to sin (ἁμαρτίας), not to the masculine νόμον; rendered 'come out from sin'.

Spirit/spirit: in Romans 8:2 and Galatians 6:8 Cyril reads πνεῦμα as the spiritual will of the human mind (τὸ θέλημα τὸ πνευματικόν), its inclination toward the good, so 'spirit' is printed lowercase; the Holy Spirit, named separately, is capitalised.
